items: You're on the money about the flows. The stage-based rebuild, the quiz, the subscription flows and switching SMS off: I'd like to do all four, inside the current retainer.
On unsubscribes you're right, and the source surprised me. Campaigns are 85% of them by volume, but the flows lose people 2.6x faster per email sent, so the rebuild you want fixes list burn too.
The one bit I'd tweak is the volume cut. Your heaviest weeks have the lowest unsubscribe rate (-0.54 correlation), and the five worst weeks of the year were all one and two send weeks.
Last quarter you sent 36% more and earned 27% more, at better revenue per recipient and a lower unsubscribe rate. I think that's the experiment already run for us.
Good news on list health: there isn't much left to trim. Campaigns already go to a 90-day-engaged segment with seven exclusion lists on top, not the 677,227-profile file.

So what if we tweak it this way? Hold the cadence, put the effort into targeting and the flow rebuild, and add an evergreen best-of flow. On your own numbers, cutting three quarters of the campaigns would cost about $483.0k a year.
blocks.label: The short of it

blocks.html:
Where I landed

First, thank you for this. Pulling Meta, Google, Shopify, Klaviyo and the P&L into one view is the part almost everyone skips, and your read on the business is right: paid is at its ceiling, so retention is the constraint now. I agree with nearly all of it.

Three of your four asks I'd just get on with. The fourth, campaign cadence, is the one where the data took me somewhere slightly different from where I expected, so let me show you what I found and then suggest a tweak rather than a change of direction.

Where your unsubscribes are coming from

You're right that the volume sits with campaigns: 67,130 over the last 12 months against 11,563 from flows.

What I didn't expect is what happens per email delivered. Flows unsubscribe at 0.60% against 0.23% for campaigns, so 2.6 times the rate. Campaigns lead the total because they send far more, not because they upset more people. The heaviest single losses in the account are flow messages: ZM // Welcome Flow at 0.78%, ZM // Welcome Flow (SMS) PHASING OUT at 4.44%, ZM // Abandoned Browse at 0.77%. In my opinion that makes your flow rebuild worth even more than you pitched it, because it fixes list burn at the same time as the earnings.

blocks.cap: 52 weeks, Sep ’25 to Aug ’26. Bars are what the week earned, the line is the unsubscribe rate per recipient at that cadence.
blocks.title: What each cadence earns, and what it costs in unsubscribes

blocks.html:
The one bit I'd tweak

Here's what made me pause. Sends per week against the unsubscribe rate is -0.54, so the weeks with more campaigns in them have a lower rate per recipient, not a higher one. The five worst weeks of the year were all one and two send weeks, and the six and seven send weeks are the cleanest in the account. Cadence does drive the unsubscribe count (+0.64), but only because it drives volume.

And I think the last two quarters have run the test for us. From Mar ’26 you sent 44 campaigns and earned $138,568 at $0.0177 per recipient and a 0.191% unsubscribe rate. In the quarter to Aug ’26 you sent 60, up 36%, and earned $175,389, up 27%, at $0.0232 per recipient and 0.183%. More sending came with better revenue per recipient and a slightly lower unsubscribe rate, in the same window this review covers.

With the account's own growth taken out, sends against weekly revenue is +0.72 and sends against revenue per campaign is -0.17, which reads as no measurable decline in what a single campaign earns as volume rises. So my honest read is that going to a quarter of the volume would take roughly three quarters of the campaign revenue with it, and I don't think it would move the unsubscribe rate much at all.

blocks.cap: 70 email campaigns over the last 120 days, each a bar. The line is the median at 0.183%.
blocks.title: Every campaign's unsubscribe rate, worst to best

blocks.html:
I went looking for a culprit and couldn't find one

Before taking any of that as read I checked whether a few bad sends were doing the damage. Across 70 campaigns the rate runs from 0.108% to 0.294%, median 0.183%, and the worst single campaign is only 2.5% of the period's unsubscribes. Nothing broken, no offender to pull. It looks like this is simply what a send to a warm list costs.

Worth knowing: who your campaigns already reach

This one is easy to misread from recipient counts alone, so I went and checked the audiences. Campaigns go to ZM // 90D Engaged + Apple Privacy False (201,504 profiles), 10 of the last 15 sends, each one also excluding DA | 4+ Soft Bounces, ZM // List Hygiene - Bad Emails, ZM // List Hygiene - Dead (180 Days), ZM // List Hygiene - Engagement Exclusion: 10 Emails and more. Against a file of 677,227 profiles, you're already mailing a tightly filtered slice rather than the list.

Which I think is good news. The 0.23% you pay is being paid on people who engaged in the last 90 days, and that reads as a normal cost rather than a symptom. It also means there isn't a suppression win sitting there waiting to be taken.

There is room in the other direction though. Campaigns go to the 90-day engaged group, while the 180-day engaged group is 254,040 people. So there are roughly 52,536 people who engaged in the last three to six months and currently hear nothing from us, which is where the last idea below goes.

What I think we should do, and it's more work not less

1. Rebuild the stage-based flows, prioritised by cohort size. Completely agree, and I'd start here. They're the weakest per-recipient performers in the account sitting in front of its highest-intent audience, and they're also among the worst for unsubscribes, so the rebuild pays twice.

2. On cadence, what if we hold it and fix the targeting instead? Your stage-targeted sends already earn $0.0274 per recipient against $0.0226 for the wider engaged sends, +21% better. So I think the lever is which people get which campaign rather than how many campaigns go out. Your own segmenting is also the best evidence I have that the stage-based flows are going to work.

3. An evergreen best-of flow, taking proven campaigns to people we don't currently reach. The ten best campaigns of the last 120 days averaged $0.0305 per recipient against a $0.0221 median, at a 0.201% unsubscribe rate, below the account average. Right now that content goes out once and stops. On a flow it keeps earning, and it gives us something worth sending to those 52,536 warm people who sit outside the campaign audience. One heads-up so it doesn't surprise you later: it will pull the average revenue per recipient across the flows down, because it's a campaign travelling on a flow rail. The revenue it adds is still additional.

4. Quiz reach, subscription coverage, and SMS. Agreed on all three. The quiz is the best-performing thing in the account and it's reaching almost nobody, the subscription flow reaching 4,728 people against roughly 12,000 orders a month reads to me like a trigger fault rather than a performance one, and SMS should come off until it's rebuilt. That last one is the place where I think sending less is clearly right.

What this costs you. Nothing. The flow rebuild, the evergreen build and the campaign work all come inside the current rate. We've been getting more efficient and I'd rather put that back into the account than into our margin. Let's look at scope again in six months, once the flows are rebuilt and we can see what they're doing.

52 weeks of your own campaign sends, Sep ’25 to Aug ’26, grouped by campaigns per week, plus every email campaign of the last 120 days at individual level. Unsubscribes are split by source using each channel's own delivered volume, so the rates are per email sent rather than per person on the list.

Correlations are Pearson. The revenue ones are detrended, which takes the straight-line growth in the account out of both sides before comparing them, so "busier weeks earned more" can't be mistaken for "sending more changed what a send earns". Revenue is Klaviyo attributed on last click, so treat it as the generous reading rather than the truth. A holdout is the only way to get the strict number and I'm happy to run one whenever you want it.

reports.summary: Where your unsubscribes are really coming from, the one bit of the plan I'd tweak, and the four things I'd like to get on with. All inside the current retainer.
